CBS News live updates

Updated on:  October 13, 2026 / 1:37 PM EDT
            / CBS News

Suspected cholera cases in Yemen have tripled in three weeks, the World Health Organization said Tuesday, warning that the growing disease burden was straining hospitals already treating an increasing number of war casualties.

The country's escalating war, combined with mass displacement, is helping infectious disease outbreaks spread, the WHO said, with overcrowding, inadequate access to safe water and disrupted health services exposing more people to cholera, measles and other preventable diseases.

Suspected cholera cases tripled from 217 in the week beginning Sept. 6, to 647 in the week beginning Sept. 27, the U.N. health agency said.

It said Yemeni authorities have reported 8,034 suspected cases and 27 cholera deaths this year – with a quarter of the suspected cases occurring in the last four weeks alone.

"Families fleeing conflict are now facing another threat from diseases that can be prevented and treated," said Annette Heinzelmann, the WHO's emergency director for the region. "Without urgent funding and unimpeded access to safe water, vaccination and essential health services, outbreaks could spread rapidly among already vulnerable communities."

The United Kingdom is advising against all but essential travel to large areas of Saudi Arabia, including the capital city of Riyadh, in the wake of Houthi strikes.

The new warning, released Tuesday, also included several areas the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office warned should be avoided entirely. The area to be avoided entirely is within about 6 miles of the Yemeni border with Saudi Arabia, according to the U.K. Nonessential travel is not advised to Aseer, Riyadh, Najran and Jizan provinces.

The U.S. has issued similar advisories for travel to Saudi Arabia, banning all government employees from being within 20 miles of the Yemeni border and advising against all U.S. citizens visiting that area.

The U.S. also "strongly recommends" citizens avoid King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and the surrounding areas in the wake of a Houthi attack on Saturday that killed 13 people.

President Trump would not say whether he'll join Saudi Arabia in launching strikes against the Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen when leaving the White House on Tuesday afternoon but he did later send a Truth Social threatening the group.

"The Houthis are behaving very badly. I thought they learned their lesson a year ago when we bombed the HELL out of them and, at their request, stopped," Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social. "They've been silent for a long time, but now they've emerged again, probably at the behest of Iran."

The president said the Houthis came back "in a very nasty way, hitting Saudi Arabia, and purposefully trying to drive up Oil prices, probably prior to the U.S. Elections — NOT NICE."

The Houthis have struck multiple airports in the last week, including a strike Saturday against Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport that killed 13 people.

Mr. Trump said he had spoken with Saudi leader Mohammed bin Salman, but would not say whether he'd decided to join the Saudi campaign against the Houthis.

"I can't tell you that," the president said from the White House South Lawn, while leaving for a trip to Alaska. "Do you really think I can tell you that? I'd love to tell you, but I'm not going to tell you that."

The U.S. launched multiple strikes against Houthi targets in Yemen from March to May 2025. More than 150 innocent civilians were also killed in those strikes, according to a report released by the Pentagon this August.

Saudi-led forces carried out airstrikes on oil facilities west of Sanaa, Yemen's Houthi-held capital, Houthi-linked TV network Al-Masirah reported Tuesday. The report did not provide any evidence of the strikes.

It came shortly after a warning was issued by the Saudi-led military coalition spokesman to residents in part of Sanaa to evacuate for their safety. Witnesses in the city reported explosions in Sanaa. It was not immediately clear what was hit.

Houthi military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said on X that the Iran-backed group's forces were "confronting the Saudi enemy's combat formations that are targeting the capital, Sanaa."

The Houthis warned Tuesday that if Saudi Arabia attacked Sanaa, they would retaliate against Saudi Aramco facilities and the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.

The Iran-backed Houthis issued an evacuation warning Tuesday to civilians near all facilities belonging to Saudi Arabia's state-run energy giant Saudi Aramco.

In a post on X, Houthi military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said the group wished to "warn all employees and citizens present near any facility belonging to Aramco to evacuate it and move away, as it is a legitimate target for our forces."

It came after a warning issued earlier Tuesday by the Saudi-led military coalition to civilians in parts of Yemen's Houthi-held capital, Sanaa, to evacuate ahead of what it said would be a "targeted operation."

The Houthis warned Saudi Arabia Tuesday that any strikes on the Yemeni capital would trigger a "harsh and painful" retaliation.

"Any strikes on the capital, Sanaa, will be met with a harsh and painful response in the capital of the Saudi enemy, Riyadh," Houthi military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree warned in a post on X.

An hour later he expanded on the threat, saying in another post that if Saudi Arabia "proceeds with its announced targeting" of Sanaa, the Iran-backed rebels would attack state energy company Saudi Aramco's headquarters in Damman, along with King Khalid Airport in Riyadh, which they have already targeted with deadly missile strikes, and Aramco's refinery in Riyadh.

The escalating conflict between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition fighting on behalf of Yemen's government has spiralled over the past week, with a series of Houthi strikes reaching Saudi airports, killing at least 20 people.

The Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen said Tuesday that it was poised to issue an evacuation warning for civilians in part of Sanaa, the war-torn nation's capital city, which has been held by the Iran-backed rebels for more than a decade.

"A warning will be imminently issued for civilians to evacuate a site in Sanaa ahead of a targeted operation," coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki said in a post on X.

Saudi Arabia has been hit by repeated and deadly Houthi strikes over the last week, as it continues targeting areas held by the rebels near the Yemen-Saudi border, as well as along its Red Sea coast.

Saudi Arabia's public missile warning system went silent days before the Houthis launched a series of deadly strikes on the kingdom last week, the Reuters news agency reported Tuesday.

The system stopped working before Houthi missile strikes on Saudi airports killed 20 people - most of them over last weekend at the capital's King Khalid International Airport.

Saudi Arabia has launched an investigation to determine how its air defenses failed to intercept the recent barrages of Houthi missiles and drones, two regional officials speaking on condition of anonymity told the Associated Press Tuesday.

The Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthis said Tuesday that its forces had intercepted three drones north of the Saudi capital, Riyadh.

"Interception and destruction of 3 drones north of Riyadh city," Major General Turki al-Maliki, a spokesman for the coalition, wrote on X.

The reported drone interceptions, however, come after a week of deadly Houthi missile attacks, which appear to have evaded Saudi defenses with alarming regularity.

At least 20 people were killed over the last week in Houthi strikes on Saudi airports, including 13 killed in a single missile strike Saturday on King Khalid International, in the capital city Riyadh.

President Trump said he does not believe China and Russia are helping Iran, adding they have "too much to lose."

Responding to comments that China and Russia may be assisting Iran, Mr. Trump said in a Truth Social post: "If they are, it's at a very low level, but I don't believe they are at all."

"They have too much to lose, and we would know about it, and know about it very fast!" he added.

Mr. Trump said in July that he did not believe China and Russia were selling weapons to Iran, warning that "it would be very bad for them" if they did.

The Kremlin has previously denied reports that Russia was sharing intel with Iran, while China has denied reports that the country's top semiconductor firm has sent chipmaking tools to Iran.

Both countries have also been accused of helping Iran circumvent sanctions on its oil sales.

In August, the U.S. Treasury announced a wave of economic sanctions targeting Iran's allies, namely China and Iran.
